blocks.text: 1. overview
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444059885-7850253.png

The six metrics already covered in this module have each offered a genuinely different lens on regression model quality: MAE, MSE, RMSE, and RMSLE all report error in some unit, or transformed unit, tied directly to the target, while R² and Adjusted R² instead report a dimensionless, variance-explained ratio. Mean Absolute Percentage Error, MAPE for short, closes this module with yet another distinct lens: error expressed as a plain, everyday percentage, arguably the single most immediately intuitive way to communicate model accuracy to a non-technical audience.

MAPE builds directly on MAE's familiar structure, average absolute error, already covered as the very first topic in this module, but reframes that error as a percentage of the actual value rather than as a raw, unit-bound number. This closing topic examines both MAPE's genuine communicative strengths and its real, important mathematical limitations, several of which make it a poor choice for certain kinds of targets despite its surface-level appeal.
2. The Formula
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444059885-460242889.png

MAPE is computed through a direct extension of MAE's own calculation, already covered in the first topic of this module. For every single prediction, first compute the absolute error exactly as MAE does, the absolute value of actual minus predicted. Then divide that absolute error by the actual value itself, and multiply by 100 to express the result as a percentage.

Finally, average these individual percentage errors across every example in the evaluation dataset. Formally, MAPE equals the average of the absolute value of actual minus predicted, divided by actual, multiplied by 100 percent. The resulting single number represents, on average, what percentage off the model's predictions tend to be, relative to the true values they were predicting.
3. Building Directly on MAE
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444060428-101350836.png

It is worth being explicit about how closely MAPE mirrors MAE's own structure, since recognizing this connection makes MAPE easy to understand quickly. Where MAE reports the average absolute error in raw units, MAPE applies that exact same averaging structure, just after first dividing each individual absolute error by its corresponding actual value, converting each raw error into a percentage before the averaging step happens.

This reframing directly answers a specific, commonly asked question: on average, what percentage off are the model's predictions? This is a framing nearly everyone intuitively understands without requiring any statistics background at all, arguably even more immediately graspable than MAE's already quite interpretable raw-unit result, since percentages are a nearly universal way of communicating proportional accuracy in everyday, non-technical contexts.
4. A Different Route to Scale Independence

R², covered two topics ago, achieved scale independence by expressing model quality as a dimensionless ratio of explained to total variance. MAPE achieves a broadly similar practical benefit, comparability across entirely different targets and scales, through a genuinely different mechanism: expressing error as a percentage of the actual value, rather than as a variance ratio.

A MAPE of 10 percent carries essentially the same practical meaning, predictions are off by about 10 percent on average, whether the underlying model is predicting prices in dollars, temperatures in degrees, or quantities in units, a comparability advantage MAE and RMSE, reported in raw, unit-bound terms, cannot offer directly on their own. This makes MAPE a genuinely useful complement to MAE and RMSE specifically when comparability across different scales or different problems matters for the evaluation being performed.

blocks.text: 5. A Serious Limitation: Division by Zero

blocks.alt: A Serious Limitation: Division by Zero
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444060429-219704548.png

MAPE's formula divides by the actual value for every single prediction, and this creates a serious, genuinely important mathematical limitation worth understanding directly before using this metric on any real problem. Whenever an actual value is exactly zero, that specific division is mathematically undefined, division by zero, and the entire MAPE calculation for that example, and often the whole averaged result, simply breaks down.

Even when the actual value is not exactly zero but merely very close to it, a small, arguably unremarkable absolute error can produce an enormous, wildly misleading percentage error for that one example, since dividing by a tiny number inflates the resulting percentage dramatically. This is not a rare or theoretical edge case; many real-world regression targets, sales counts, website visits, inventory levels, can legitimately take a value of exactly zero or very close to it, making this limitation a genuinely practical concern, not just a mathematical curiosity.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Before using MAPE on any dataset, explicitly check whether the target contains zero or near-zero values. If it does, MAPE is likely the wrong metric choice entirely, and MAE, RMSE, or RMSLE, all covered earlier in this module, remain viable, well-defined alternatives.

blocks.text: 6. An Asymmetric Penalty Structure
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444060429-80153609.png

MAPE has a second, more subtle limitation worth understanding directly: it penalizes overestimation and underestimation asymmetrically, in a way that can genuinely distort model comparisons. Consider predicting 150 when the actual value is 100, an overestimate, which produces a 50 percent error, and predicting 50 when the actual value is 100, an underestimate of the same raw magnitude, which also produces a 50 percent error, seemingly symmetric so far.

But push the comparison further: predicting 200 when the actual value is 100 produces a 100 percent error, while predicting 0 when the actual value is 100 also produces exactly 100 percent, the mathematical maximum an underestimate can ever reach, since a prediction cannot go below zero without becoming a negative number relative to a positive actual value. Overestimates, by contrast, have no such ceiling at all and can in principle produce percentage errors of 200 percent, 500 percent, or more. This creates a genuine, structural asymmetry: MAPE's percentage-error scale allows unbounded penalties for overestimation but caps underestimation penalties at 100 percent, a distortion worth being aware of when interpreting or comparing MAPE results.
7. Outlier Sensitivity, Driven by Small Actual Values

blocks.alt: Outlier Sensitivity, Driven by Small Actual Values
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444060429-334425749.png

MAPE has its own distinct version of outlier sensitivity, related to but genuinely different from the outlier sensitivity already covered for MSE and RMSE earlier in this module. Rather than being driven by unusually large errors, as MSE and RMSE are, MAPE's outlier sensitivity is driven by unusually small actual values, exactly the scenario covered in the Division by Zero section: a single actual value very close to zero can produce a massive individual percentage error, even from a fairly ordinary, unremarkable absolute error.

That one massive percentage error can then dominate the final averaged MAPE almost entirely, in much the same spirit as a single extreme error dominates MSE, but triggered here by a small actual value rather than a large raw error. This is a genuinely different, additional failure mode worth checking for specifically whenever using MAPE, distinct from, though conceptually related to, the outlier concerns already covered for MSE and RMSE.
8. When MAPE Is the Right Choice

blocks.alt: When MAPE Is the Right Choice
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444060430-802816209.png

MAPE is a strong, natural choice specifically when the target values are reliably positive and meaningfully away from zero across the entire evaluation dataset, situations like sales forecasting, demand planning, and many standard business key performance indicators, where percentage-based accuracy targets, being within 10 percent of the true value, are already the natural, familiar way results get discussed and communicated within that domain.

It is also the natural choice whenever the primary goal is communicating accuracy to a non-technical audience as simply and intuitively as possible, since a percentage is arguably the single most universally understood way to express proportional accuracy without requiring any statistical background at all. Whenever the target can legitimately be zero or very close to zero, however, MAPE should be avoided entirely, in favor of MAE, RMSE, or RMSLE, all covered earlier in this module and all well-defined regardless of how close to zero the target happens to be.

blocks.text: 9. Worked Example
The example below computes MAPE for house price predictions and directly demonstrates the division-by-zero problem on a different target that legitimately includes zero values.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_percentage_error

# House prices: reliably positive, meaningfully away from zero, a good MAPE candidate
actual_prices = np.array([250, 310, 180, 420, 275, 390, 205])
predicted_prices = np.array([245, 305, 190, 400, 280, 375, 210])

mape = mean_absolute_percentage_error(actual_prices, predicted_prices)
print(f"House price MAPE: {mape * 100:.2f}%")

# Daily units sold: can legitimately be zero, a poor MAPE candidate
actual_sales = np.array([12, 8, 0, 15, 3, 0, 20])   # two days with zero sales, entirely legitimate
predicted_sales = np.array([10, 9, 1, 14, 4, 1, 18])

try:
    sales_mape = mean_absolute_percentage_error(actual_sales, predicted_sales)
    print(f"Daily sales MAPE: {sales_mape * 100:.2f}%")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"MAPE calculation issue: {e}")

# Show how the zero-actual days individually distort the percentage calculation
individual_pct_errors = np.abs(actual_sales - predicted_sales) / np.where(actual_sales == 0, np.nan, actual_sales)
print("\nIndividual percentage errors (NaN where actual sales were zero):")
print(np.round(individual_pct_errors * 100, 1))

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: scikit-learn's mean_absolute_percentage_error handles zero actual values by treating them as a very large denominator internally rather than raising an outright error, but the resulting MAPE value is still heavily distorted by those zero-actual days, exactly the practical concern covered throughout this topic.

blocks.text: 10. Key Takeaways

items: MAPE extends MAE's structure by dividing each absolute error by the actual value, expressing error as a percentage.
It offers an immediately intuitive, non-technical way to communicate model accuracy, arguably the most accessible metric in this module.
Like R², it achieves scale independence and cross-problem comparability, though through a different mechanism, percentages rather than variance ratios.
It is mathematically undefined when the actual value is exactly zero, and badly distorted when the actual value is close to zero.
It has an asymmetric penalty structure: underestimation caps at 100 percent, while overestimation has no upper bound.
It has its own distinct outlier sensitivity, driven by unusually small actual values rather than by unusually large errors.
MAPE fits reliably positive, away-from-zero targets and non-technical, percentage-based communication of results.
Avoid MAPE entirely whenever the target can legitimately be zero or very close to zero; use MAE, RMSE, or RMSLE instead.
